newsitem.title: CANADA: WIC says may sell CTV shares to Baton.
newsitem.headline: WIC says may sell CTV shares to Baton.

text.p: Canadian broadcaster WIC Western International Communications Ltd said Friday it was considering selling its share in the CTV television network to rival Baton Broadcasting Inc.

If Canada's federal broadcast regulator approves two deals, Baton will become the controlling shareholder of CTV. This will trigger a 'put' clause giving WIC 30 days in which to sell its shares to Baton.

WIC Chief Executive John Lacey told a conference call that WIC was considering selling its share under the put option if the Baton deals are approved. Analysts have said the deal is likely to win approval.
Lacey said a CRTC decision is likely by early September. At that point, WIC will review the terms for the CRTC's approval and "assess our options then."

But he stressed that even if WIC decides to sell its share in CTV the decision would not affect the affiliation agreements among many of its TV stations and the network. Those run through the end of 1999.
With the acquisition of a Quebec station, WIC now reaches all of Canada's major English language markets. "We see ourselves today as a national network," Lacey said.

Lacey told the call that he has set an objective of matching or slightly exceeding last year's net earnings this year despite C$8.3 million in pre-tax restructuring charges. "I'd say we're heading for a reasonable year," he said.

WIC on Thursday reported earnings of C$13.3 million for the first nine months of its 1997 fiscal year after C$4.5 million in restructuring costs. This compared to C$13.5 million in the same period a year earlier.
WIC's TV operations are performing strongly, he said.

Canadian Satellite Communications Inc, of which WIC owns 54 percent, will be reviewing its business plan in the fourth quarter and Lacey said he did not know if this would entail strategy changes or financial restructuring.
WIC's is now ready to begin field testing its local multipoint communications service called Connexus after initial tests have shown the technology is working, Lacey said.
